{"evidence": "Theorem: For every integer n >= 1, S_n = sum_{j=1}^n (2j - 1) = n^2.

Proof by mathematical induction on n.

Base case: Let n = 1. Then S_1 = 2(1) - 1 = 1 = 1^2. Thus the statement holds for n = 1.

Induction hypothesis: Fix an arbitrary integer k >= 1 and assume that S_k = sum_{j=1}^k (2j - 1) = k^2.

Induction step: We must prove that S_{k+1} = (k + 1)^2. By the definition of a finite sum,

S_{k+1} = sum_{j=1}^{k+1} (2j - 1)
 = sum_{j=1}^k (2j - 1) + (2(k + 1) - 1)
 = S_k + (2k + 1).

Applying the induction hypothesis S_k = k^2 gives

S_{k+1} = k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2.

Therefore, whenever the statement holds for k, it also holds for k + 1.

Conclusion: The base case and induction step establish, by the principle of mathematical induction, that sum_{j=1}^n (2j - 1) = n^2 for every integer n >= 1. QED.

Hypotheses: n is a positive integer; k is an arbitrary positive integer in the induction step; the induction hypothesis is assumed only for the purpose of proving the next case. {"evidence": "Theorem: sqrt(2) is irrational.

Proof by contradiction.

Assume that sqrt(2) is rational. Then there exist integers p and q, with q != 0 and gcd(|p|,|q|) = 1, such that sqrt(2) = p/q. Squaring both sides gives

p^2 = 2q^2. (1)

We first establish the parity lemma: if n is an integer and n^2 is even, then n is even.

Proof of the lemma: Suppose n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k, so

n^2 = (2k + 1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1.

Thus n^2 is odd. By contraposition, if n^2 is even, then n is even. This proves the lemma.

Returning to (1), the integer p^2 equals 2q^2 and is therefore even. By the parity lemma, p must be even. Hence p = 2k for some integer k.

Substituting this expression into (1) gives

4k^2 = 2q^2.

Dividing by 2 yields

q^2 = 2k^2. (2)

Equation (2) shows that q^2 is even. Applying the same parity lemma again, q must be even. Thus q = 2m for some integer m.

Consequently, 2 divides both p and q, so gcd(|p|,|q|) >= 2. This contradicts the original assumption that gcd(|p|,|q|) = 1.

Therefore no representation sqrt(2) = p/q by integers p and q with q != 0 is possible. Hence sqrt(2) is irrational. QED.

{"evidence": "THEOREM 1: Algebraic difference-of-squares identity.

Claim: For every integer j,

2j - 1 = j^2 - (j - 1)^2.

Proof: Expanding the square gives

(j - 1)^2 = j^2 - 2j + 1.

Consequently,

j^2 - (j - 1)^2 = j^2 - (j^2 - 2j + 1) = 2j - 1.

This is an exact algebraic identity. In fact, it holds in any commutative ring with identity, although only integer values are needed here.

THEOREM 2: Telescoping proof of the odd-integer sum formula.

Claim: For every integer n >= 0,

S_n := sum_{j=1}^n (2j - 1) = n^2.

Proof: First suppose n >= 1. Applying Theorem 1 term by term,

S_n = sum_{j=1}^n [j^2 - (j - 1)^2].

Writing out this finite sum explicitly,

S_n = (1^2 - 0^2) + (2^2 - 1^2) + (3^2 - 2^2) + ... + (n^2 - (n - 1)^2).

Each intermediate square appears exactly twice, once positively and once negatively, and therefore cancels. The only remaining terms are n^2 and -0^2. Thus

S_n = n^2 - 0^2 = n^2.

Equivalently, by finite-sum linearity and an index shift,

S_n = sum_{j=1}^n j^2 - sum_{j=1}^n (j - 1)^2
 = sum_{j=1}^n j^2 - sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^2
 = n^2 - 0^2
 = n^2.

The cancellation is valid because the two finite sums have precisely the common terms 1^2 through (n - 1)^2.

Boundary case n = 0: By the empty-sum convention,

S_0 = sum_{j=1}^0 (2j - 1) = 0 = 0^2.

Therefore the formula holds for all integers n >= 0. No induction is used.

THEOREM 3: Generalized interval identity.

Claim: For arbitrary integers a and b satisfying 0 <= a <= b,

sum_{j=a+1}^b (2j - 1) = b^2 - a^2.

Proof: Suppose first that a < b. Applying Theorem 1,

sum_{j=a+1}^b (2j - 1)
= sum_{j=a+1}^b [j^2 - (j - 1)^2]
= [(a + 1)^2 - a^2] + [(a + 2)^2 - (a + 1)^2] + ... + [b^2 - (b - 1)^2].

All intermediate squares cancel in pairs, leaving

sum_{j=a+1}^b (2j - 1) = b^2 - a^2.

An equivalent calculation uses Theorem 2:

sum_{j=a+1}^b (2j - 1)
= sum_{j=1}^b (2j - 1) - sum_{j=1}^a (2j - 1)
= b^2 - a^2.

Boundary case a = b: The lower index becomes b + 1, so the sum is empty. Hence

sum_{j=b+1}^b (2j - 1) = 0 = b^2 - b^2.

Thus the generalized identity holds whenever 0 <= a <= b.

Recovery of the original identity: Set a = 0 and b = n, where n >= 0. The generalized formula becomes

sum_{j=1}^n (2j - 1) = n^2 - 0^2 = n^2.

THEOREM 4: Equivalent zero-indexed formulation.

Claim: For every integer n >= 0,

sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (2j + 1) = n^2.

Proof: For n >= 1, introduce the new index k = j + 1, equivalently j = k - 1. The original index range 0 <= j <= n - 1 becomes 1 <= k <= n. Moreover,

2j + 1 = 2(k - 1) + 1 = 2k - 1.

Consequently,

sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (2j + 1)
= sum_{k=1}^n (2k - 1)
= n^2,

where the final equality follows from Theorem 2.

For n = 0, the zero-indexed sum is sum_{j=0}^{-1} (2j + 1), which is empty under the standard convention and therefore equals 0 = 0^2.

This establishes the equivalent formulation for every integer n >= 0.

{"evidence": "PART I. IRRATIONALITY OF sqrt(2) BY INFINITE DESCENT

Theorem 1. sqrt(2) is irrational.

Proof. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that sqrt(2) is rational. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.

Define S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.

Our assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.

Squaring gives

(1) p^2 = 2q^2.

We invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.

For completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.

Equation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.

Substituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence

(2) q^2 = 2r^2.

Therefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.

We have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).

Thus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.

The contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.

The argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.

PART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS

Lemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.

Proof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.

Suppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.

The lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.

Theorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.

Proof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.

Squaring gives

(3) p^2 = l q^2.

Thus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.

Substituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives

(4) q^2 = l k^2.

Consequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.

Therefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.

Hence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.

Primality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.

For comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.

PART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS

Theorem 4. For every integer m >= 0, sqrt(m) is rational if and only if m is the square of an integer.

Proof.

Case 1: m = 0.

We have sqrt(0) = 0, which is rational, and 0 = 0^2, so 0 is a perfect square. Therefore both directions of the equivalence hold.

Case 2: m >= 1.

First assume sqrt(m) is rational. Since sqrt(m) > 0, write

sqrt(m) = a/b,

where a and b are positive integers and gcd(a,b) = 1.

Squaring yields

(5) a^2 = mb^2.

We invoke the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n >= 2 has a factorization into prime powers, and that factorization is unique up to the ordering of the primes. The integer 1 corresponds to the empty prime product.

For each prime r and positive integer n, define v_r(n) as the nonnegative integer exponent of r in the unique prime factorization of n. Then

v_r(xy) = v_r(x) + v_r(y)

for positive integers x and y, and in particular

v_r(x^2) = 2v_r(x).

These identities follow from uniqueness of prime factorization.

Applying v_r to both sides of (5), for any prime r, gives

v_r(a^2) = v_r(mb^2),

hence

(6) 2v_r(a) = v_r(m) + 2v_r(b).

Rearranging,

(7) v_r(m) = 2(v_r(a) - v_r(b)).

The right-hand side is an even integer. Therefore v_r(m) is even for every prime r.

This explicitly explains the exponent argument: squaring an integer doubles every prime exponent, so the prime exponents in a^2 and b^2 are all even. Equality a^2 = mb^2 forces the exponent of m, added to an even exponent from b^2, to equal an even exponent from a^2. Consequently the exponent of m itself must be even.

By the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, write

m = r_1^{e_1} r_2^{e_2} ... r_t^{e_t},

where the r_i are distinct primes and all e_i are positive integers. If m = 1, take t = 0 and interpret the product as 1.

As established, every e_i is even. Hence e_i = 2f_i for some nonnegative integer f_i.

Define

k = r_1^{f_1} r_2^{f_2} ... r_t^{f_t}.

Then k is a positive integer and

k^2 = r_1^{2f_1} r_2^{2f_2} ... r_t^{2f_t} = m.

Thus m is a perfect square.

This proves the forward implication.

Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. "evidence": "PART I. IRRATIONALITY OF sqrt(2) BY INFINITE DESCENT\n\nTheorem 1. sqrt(2) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that sqrt(2) is rational. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS\n\nLemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.\n\nProof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.\n\nSuppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(3) p^2 = l q^2.\n\nThus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.\n\nSubstituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives\n\n(4) q^2 = l k^2.\n\nConsequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.\n\nTherefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.\n\nHence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.\n\nPART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS\n\nTheorem 4. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS\n\nLemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.\n\nProof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.\n\nSuppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(3) p^2 = l q^2.\n\nThus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.\n\nSubstituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives\n\n(4) q^2 = l k^2.\n\nConsequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.\n\nTherefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.\n\nHence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.\n\nPART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS\n\nTheorem 4. For every integer m >= 0, sqrt(m) is rational if and only if m is the square of an integer.\n\nProof.\n\nCase 1: m = 0.\n\nWe have sqrt(0) = 0, which is rational, and 0 = 0^2, so 0 is a perfect square. Therefore both directions of the equivalence hold.\n\nCase 2: m >= 1.\n\nFirst assume sqrt(m) is rational. Since sqrt(m) > 0, write\n\nsqrt(m) = a/b,\n\nwhere a and b are positive integers and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n\nSquaring yields\n\n(5) a^2 = mb^2.\n\nWe invoke the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n >= 2 has a factorization into prime powers, and that factorization is unique up to the ordering of the primes. The integer 1 corresponds to the empty prime product.\n\nFor each prime r and positive integer n, define v_r(n) as the nonnegative integer exponent of r in the unique prime factorization of n. Then\n\nv_r(xy) = v_r(x) + v_r(y)\n\nfor positive integers x and y, and in particular\n\nv_r(x^2) = 2v_r(x).\n\nThese identities follow from uniqueness of prime factorization.\n\nApplying v_r to both sides of (5), for any prime r, gives\n\nv_r(a^2) = v_r(mb^2),\n\nhence\n\n(6) 2v_r(a) = v_r(m) + 2v_r(b).\n\nRearranging,\n\n(7) v_r(m) = 2(v_r(a) - v_r(b)).\n\nThe right-hand side is an even integer. Therefore v_r(m) is even for every prime r.\n\nThis explicitly explains the exponent argument: squaring an integer doubles every prime exponent, so the prime exponents in a^2 and b^2 are all even. Equality a^2 = mb^2 forces the exponent of m, added to an even exponent from b^2, to equal an even exponent from a^2. Consequently the exponent of m itself must be even.\n\nBy the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, write\n\nm = r_1^{e_1} r_2^{e_2} ... r_t^{e_t},\n\nwhere the r_i are distinct primes and all e_i are positive integers. If m = 1, take t = 0 and interpret the product as 1.\n\nAs established, every e_i is even. Hence e_i = 2f_i for some nonnegative integer f_i.\n\nDefine\n\nk = r_1^{f_1} r_2^{f_2} ... r_t^{f_t}.\n\nThen k is a positive integer and\n\nk^2 = r_1^{2f_1} r_2^{2f_2} ... r_t^{2f_t} = m.\n\nThus m is a perfect square.\n\nThis proves the forward implication.\n\nConversely, suppose m is the square of an integer z. Then m = z^2. The nonnegative real square root satisfies sqrt(m) = |z|, which is an integer and therefore rational.\n\nThis proves the converse.\n\nCombining both cases establishes the theorem for every nonnegative integer m. QED.\n\nAdditional observation. Although we assumed gcd(a,b) = 1 as requested, equations (6) and (7) do not use coprimality. "evidence": "PART I. IRRATIONALITY OF sqrt(2) BY INFINITE DESCENT\n\nTheorem 1. sqrt(2) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that sqrt(2) is rational. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS\n\nLemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.\n\nProof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.\n\nSuppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(3) p^2 = l q^2.\n\nThus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.\n\nSubstituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives\n\n(4) q^2 = l k^2.\n\nConsequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.\n\nTherefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.\n\nHence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.\n\nPART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS\n\nTheorem 4. For every integer m >= 0, sqrt(m) is rational if and only if m is the square of an integer.\n\nProof.\n\nCase 1: m = 0.\n\nWe have sqrt(0) = 0, which is rational, and 0 = 0^2, so 0 is a perfect square. Therefore both directions of the equivalence hold.\n\nCase 2: m >= 1.\n\nFirst assume sqrt(m) is rational. Since sqrt(m) > 0, write\n\nsqrt(m) = a/b,\n\nwhere a and b are positive integers and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n\nSquaring yields\n\n(5) a^2 = mb^2.\n\nWe invoke the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n >= 2 has a factorization into prime powers, and that factorization is unique up to the ordering of the primes. The integer 1 corresponds to the empty prime product.\n\nFor each prime r and positive integer n, define v_r(n) as the nonnegative integer exponent of r in the unique prime factorization of n. Then\n\nv_r(xy) = v_r(x) + v_r(y)\n\nfor positive integers x and y, and in particular\n\nv_r(x^2) = 2v_r(x).\n\nThese identities follow from uniqueness of prime factorization.\n\nApplying v_r to both sides of (5), for any prime r, gives\n\nv_r(a^2) = v_r(mb^2),\n\nhence\n\n(6) 2v_r(a) = v_r(m) + 2v_r(b).\n\nRearranging,\n\n(7) v_r(m) = 2(v_r(a) - v_r(b)).\n\nThe right-hand side is an even integer. Therefore v_r(m) is even for every prime r.\n\nThis explicitly explains the exponent argument: squaring an integer doubles every prime exponent, so the prime exponents in a^2 and b^2 are all even. Equality a^2 = mb^2 forces the exponent of m, added to an even exponent from b^2, to equal an even exponent from a^2. Consequently the exponent of m itself must be even.\n\nBy the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, write\n\nm = r_1^{e_1} r_2^{e_2} ... r_t^{e_t},\n\nwhere the r_i are distinct primes and all e_i are positive integers. If m = 1, take t = 0 and interpret the product as 1.\n\nAs established, every e_i is even. Hence e_i = 2f_i for some nonnegative integer f_i.\n\nDefine\n\nk = r_1^{f_1} r_2^{f_2} ... r_t^{f_t}.\n\nThen k is a positive integer and\n\nk^2 = r_1^{2f_1} r_2^{2f_2} ... r_t^{2f_t} = m.\n\nThus m is a perfect square.\n\nThis proves the forward implication.\n\nConversely, suppose m is the square of an integer z. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS\n\nLemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.\n\nProof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.\n\nSuppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(3) p^2 = l q^2.\n\nThus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.\n\nSubstituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives\n\n(4) q^2 = l k^2.\n\nConsequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.\n\nTherefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.\n\nHence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.\n\nPART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS\n\nTheorem 4. For every integer m >= 0, sqrt(m) is rational if and only if m is the square of an integer.\n\nProof.\n\nCase 1: m = 0.\n\nWe have sqrt(0) = 0, which is rational, and 0 = 0^2, so 0 is a perfect square. Therefore both directions of the equivalence hold.\n\nCase 2: m >= 1.\n\nFirst assume sqrt(m) is rational. Since sqrt(m) > 0, write\n\nsqrt(m) = a/b,\n\nwhere a and b are positive integers and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n\nSquaring yields\n\n(5) a^2 = mb^2.\n\nWe invoke the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n >= 2 has a factorization into prime powers, and that factorization is unique up to the ordering of the primes. The integer 1 corresponds to the empty prime product.\n\nFor each prime r and positive integer n, define v_r(n) as the nonnegative integer exponent of r in the unique prime factorization of n. Then\n\nv_r(xy) = v_r(x) + v_r(y)\n\nfor positive integers x and y, and in particular\n\nv_r(x^2) = 2v_r(x).\n\nThese identities follow from uniqueness of prime factorization.\n\nApplying v_r to both sides of (5), for any prime r, gives\n\nv_r(a^2) = v_r(mb^2),\n\nhence\n\n(6) 2v_r(a) = v_r(m) + 2v_r(b).\n\nRearranging,\n\n(7) v_r(m) = 2(v_r(a) - v_r(b)).\n\nThe right-hand side is an even integer. Equality a^2 = mb^2 forces the exponent of m, added to an even exponent from b^2, to equal an even exponent from a^2. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS\n\nLemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.\n\nProof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.\n\nSuppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(3) p^2 = l q^2.\n\nThus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.\n\nSubstituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives\n\n(4) q^2 = l k^2.\n\nConsequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.\n\nTherefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.\n\nHence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.\n\nPART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS\n\nTheorem 4. For every integer m >= 0, sqrt(m) is rational if and only if m is the square of an integer.\n\nProof.\n\nCase 1: m = 0.\n\nWe have sqrt(0) = 0, which is rational, and 0 = 0^2, so 0 is a perfect square. Therefore both directions of the equivalence hold.\n\nCase 2: m >= 1.\n\nFirst assume sqrt(m) is rational. Since sqrt(m) > 0, write\n\nsqrt(m) = a/b,\n\nwhere a and b are positive integers and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n\nSquaring yields\n\n(5) a^2 = mb^2.\n\nWe invoke the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n >= 2 has a factorization into prime powers, and that factorization is unique up to the ordering of the primes. The integer 1 corresponds to the empty prime product.\n\nFor each prime r and positive integer n, define v_r(n) as the nonnegative integer exponent of r in the unique prime factorization of n. Then\n\nv_r(xy) = v_r(x) + v_r(y)\n\nfor positive integers x and y, and in particular\n\nv_r(x^2) = 2v_r(x).\n\nThese identities follow from uniqueness of prime factorization.\n\nApplying v_r to both sides of (5), for any prime r, gives\n\nv_r(a^2) = v_r(mb^2),\n\nhence\n\n(6) 2v_r(a) = v_r(m) + 2v_r(b).\n\nRearranging,\n\n(7) v_r(m) = 2(v_r(a) - v_r(b)).\n\nThe right-hand side is an even integer. Therefore v_r(m) is even for every prime r.\n\nThis explicitly explains the exponent argument: squaring an integer doubles every prime exponent, so the prime exponents in a^2 and b^2 are all even. Equality a^2 = mb^2 forces the exponent of m, added to an even exponent from b^2, to equal an even exponent from a^2. Consequently the exponent of m itself must be even.\n\nBy the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, write\n\nm = r_1^{e_1} r_2^{e_2} ... r_t^{e_t},\n\nwhere the r_i are distinct primes and all e_i are positive integers. If m = 1, take t = 0 and interpret the product as 1.\n\nAs established, every e_i is even. Hence e_i = 2f_i for some nonnegative integer f_i.\n\nDefine\n\nk = r_1^{f_1} r_2^{f_2} ... r_t^{f_t}.\n\nThen k is a positive integer and\n\nk^2 = r_1^{2f_1} r_2^{2f_2} ... r_t^{2f_t} = m.\n\nThus m is a perfect square.\n\nThis proves the forward implication.\n\nConversely, suppose m is the square of an integer z. Then m = z^2. The nonnegative real square root satisfies sqrt(m) = |z|, which is an integer and therefore rational.\n\nThis proves the converse.\n\nCombining both cases establishes the theorem for every nonnegative integer m. QED.\n\nAdditional observation. Although we assumed gcd(a,b) = 1 as requested, equations (6) and (7) do not use coprimality. For any positive integers a and b satisfying a^2 = mb^2, the same exponent-parity conclusion follows. Thus the prime-factorization argument is slightly stronger than the reduced-fraction formulation requires.\n\nPART IV. RELATIONSHIPS AMONG THE PROOFS\n\n1. The original parity contradiction for sqrt(2) is sufficient because p^2 = 2q^2 implies that p is even; substitution then implies that q is even. If p/q is reduced, simultaneous evenness contradicts gcd(p,q) = 1 immediately. No stronger theorem is needed.\n\n2. The infinite-descent proof replaces the reduced-fraction contradiction with minimality under the well-ordering principle. It begins with arbitrary positive-integer representations and produces a strictly smaller positive denominator. It is an alternative proof structure, but it uses exactly the same parity lemma and therefore is not algebraically independent of the original divisibility argument.\n\n3. This covers composite nonsquares that the prime-radicand theorem alone does not address.\n\n5. Theorem 4 subsumes the irrationality of sqrt(2) and sqrt(l) for prime l: any prime has exponent 1 in its own factorization and therefore is not a perfect square. Its square root must be irrational. Nevertheless, Theorems 1 and 3 give direct proofs without requiring the full characterization.\n\nPART V. BOUNDARY CASES, ASSUMPTIONS, AND INVOKED RESULTS\n\nA. Denominator positivity. A rational representation of a positive real number can always be arranged with positive numerator and denominator. The infinite-descent proof requires a positive denominator to apply well-ordering to positive integers. The denominator is never zero.\n\nB. Initial reduction. The infinite-descent proof does not assume gcd(p,q) = 1. This case is treated separately because the positive-numerator assumptions used for m >= 1 do not apply to a representation of zero.\n\nD. Unit radicand. sqrt(1) = 1. The integer 1 is a perfect square and has an empty prime factorization. The proof explicitly accommodates it.\n\nE. Negative radicands. Theorem 4 concerns real square roots and is restricted to m >= 0. For m < 0, no real number has square m, since every real square is nonnegative. Consequently the stated real-rationality question does not apply to negative radicands. The theorem makes no claim about complex square roots.\n\nF. "evidence": "PART I. IRRATIONALITY OF sqrt(2) BY INFINITE DESCENT\n\nTheorem 1. sqrt(2) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that sqrt(2) is rational. Since sqrt(2) > 0, it can be expressed as p/q with positive integers p and q. No coprimality assumption is made.\n\nDefine S = {q in Z_{>0} : there exists p in Z_{>0} such that sqrt(2) = p/q}.\n\nOur assumption implies S is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, every nonempty subset of the positive integers has a least element. Consequently, S has a smallest element q. Choose a corresponding positive integer p satisfying sqrt(2) = p/q.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(1) p^2 = 2q^2.\n\nWe invoke the elementary parity lemma: if an integer n has an even square, then n itself is even.\n\nFor completeness, this lemma follows because an odd integer n = 2k + 1 satisfies n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. The contrapositive establishes the lemma.\n\nEquation (1) shows that p^2 is even. Thus p is even, so p = 2r for some positive integer r.\n\nSubstituting gives 4r^2 = 2q^2, hence\n\n(2) q^2 = 2r^2.\n\nTherefore q^2 is even. Applying the parity lemma again, q is even. Write q = 2s for some positive integer s.\n\nWe have p/q = (2r)/(2s) = r/s = sqrt(2).\n\nThus s belongs to S. But s = q/2 satisfies 0 < s < q, contradicting the minimality of q in S.\n\nThe contradiction shows that S must be empty. Hence sqrt(2) cannot be rational. QED.\n\nThe argument does not require p/q to be reduced. Positivity ensures that the new denominator s is a positive integer, while strict decrease contradicts well-ordering. This is a genuine infinite-descent argument: a hypothetical representation forces a smaller one, so no minimal representation can exist.\n\nPART II. PRIME-DIVISIBILITY LEMMA AND PRIME RADICANDS\n\nLemma 2. Let l be a prime number and a any integer. If l divides a^2, then l divides a.\n\nProof. We invoke Euclid's lemma: if l is prime and l divides the product xy of two integers x and y, then l divides x or l divides y.\n\nSuppose l divides a^2 = a*a. Applying Euclid's lemma with x = a and y = a, we obtain l divides a or l divides a. Therefore l divides a. QED.\n\nThe lemma applies to negative integers and zero as well as positive integers. The primality assumption enters through Euclid's lemma. Without primality the assertion is false: 4 divides 2^2, but 4 does not divide 2.\n\nTheorem 3. For every prime number l, sqrt(l) is irrational.\n\nProof. Suppose sqrt(l) is rational. Since l >= 2, sqrt(l) > 0, so we can write sqrt(l) = p/q for positive integers p and q with gcd(p,q) = 1. Such a representation exists for every positive rational number after cancellation of common factors.\n\nSquaring gives\n\n(3) p^2 = l q^2.\n\nThus l divides p^2. By Lemma 2, l divides p. Hence p = lk for some positive integer k.\n\nSubstituting into (3) yields l^2 k^2 = l q^2. Since l is nonzero, division by l gives\n\n(4) q^2 = l k^2.\n\nConsequently l divides q^2. Applying Lemma 2 again, l divides q.\n\nTherefore the prime l divides both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q) = 1.\n\nHence sqrt(l) is irrational. QED.\n\nPrimality is needed precisely when inferring l divides p from l divides p^2, and similarly when inferring l divides q from l divides q^2. The remaining algebra and the final coprimality contradiction do not require primality.\n\nFor comparison, if l is composite, those divisibility inferences need not hold. For example, 4 divides 2^2 without dividing 2, and sqrt(4) = 2 is rational.\n\nPART III. COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION FOR NONNEGATIVE INTEGER RADICANDS\n\nTheorem 4. For every integer m >= 0, sqrt(m) is rational if and only if m is the square of an integer.\n\nProof.\n\nCase 1: m = 0.\n\nWe have sqrt(0) = 0, which is rational, and 0 = 0^2, so 0 is a perfect square. Therefore both directions of the equivalence hold.\n\nCase 2: m >= 1.\n\nFirst assume sqrt(m) is rational. Since sqrt(m) > 0, write\n\nsqrt(m) = a/b,\n\nwhere a and b are positive integers and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n\nSquaring yields\n\n(5) a^2 = mb^2.\n\nWe invoke the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n >= 2 has a factorization into prime powers, and that factorization is unique up to the ordering of the primes. The integer 1 corresponds to the empty prime product.\n\nFor each prime r and positive integer n, define v_r(n) as the nonnegative integer exponent of r in the unique prime factorization of n. Then\n\nv_r(xy) = v_r(x) + v_r(y)\n\nfor positive integers x and y, and in particular\n\nv_r(x^2) = 2v_r(x).\n\nThese identities follow from uniqueness of prime factorization.\n\nApplying v_r to both sides of (5), for any prime r, gives\n\nv_r(a^2) = v_r(mb^2),\n\nhence\n\n(6) 2v_r(a) = v_r(m) + 2v_r(b).\n\nRearranging,\n\n(7) v_r(m) = 2(v_r(a) - v_r(b)).\n\nThe right-hand side is an even integer. Therefore v_r(m) is even for every prime r.\n\nThis explicitly explains the exponent argument: squaring an integer doubles every prime exponent, so the prime exponents in a^2 and b^2 are all even. Equality a^2 = mb^2 forces the exponent of m, added to an even exponent from b^2, to equal an even exponent from a^2. Consequently the exponent of m itself must be even.\n\nBy the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, write\n\nm = r_1^{e_1} r_2^{e_2} ... r_t^{e_t},\n\nwhere the r_i are distinct primes and all e_i are positive integers. If m = 1, take t = 0 and interpret the product as 1.\n\nAs established, every e_i is even. Hence e_i = 2f_i for some nonnegative integer f_i.\n\nDefine\n\nk = r_1^{f_1} r_2^{f_2} ... r_t^{f_t}.\n\nThen k is a positive integer and\n\nk^2 = r_1^{2f_1} r_2^{2f_2} ... r_t^{2f_t} = m.\n\nThus m is a perfect square.\n\nThis proves the forward implication.\n\nConversely, suppose m is the square of an integer z. Then m = z^2. The nonnegative real square root satisfies sqrt(m) = |z|, which is an integer and therefore rational.\n\nThis proves the converse.\n\nCombining both cases establishes the theorem for every nonnegative integer m. QED.\n\nAdditional observation. Although we assumed gcd(a,b) = 1 as requested, equations (6) and (7) do not use coprimality. For any positive integers a and b satisfying a^2 = mb^2, the same exponent-parity conclusion follows. Thus the prime-factorization argument is slightly stronger than the reduced-fraction formulation requires.\n\nPART IV. RELATIONSHIPS AMONG THE PROOFS\n\n1.
